system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel: Buyer-Side Review of the Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter

## Headline view

The Seller calls this package "fair and balanced". It isn't. Four features combine to push most of the known risk back onto Wattlebridge:

1. The SPA limitations sweep across every claim, including title, indemnities and price mechanics.
2. Disclosure is general, and the Buyer-knowledge bar extends to anything "discoverable".
3. Several identified exposures are pushed past Completion: Riverlark, Bluefen, Ironquay and the bonuses.
4. Matters still open are described as low-risk.

The Seller's own Disclosure Letter contradicts its SPA update on several points. Clause 1.4 of that letter also says nothing in it is an admission. We should treat the Disclosure Letter as the more reliable record and use it against the update.

I have only seen the Seller's summary positions and the Disclosure Letter, not the full SPA or the DD documents. The points below should be checked against the actual drafting and the data room.

---

## A. Structural issues: the limitations regime

### 1. Title and capacity warranties under the general cap and time limit (reject)
**Seller position:** Title and capacity warranties sit under the 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) and the 18-month limit, "for administrative simplicity".

**Why it matters:** Title is the core of what we are buying. If the Seller doesn't own 100% of the shares unencumbered, we could pay AUD 24m and recover only AUD 4.8m. Capping title at 20% of the price is well outside market practice.

**Push back:**
- Fundamental warranties (title, capacity, authority, solvency, share capital) should be capped at **100% of the price**.
- They should be **excluded from the de minimis and the basket**.
- Notification should run for at least **6 years**, aligned with the NSW contract limitation period. Consider executing the SPA as a deed.

### 2. "Limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (cl 12.3/13) and "limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5) (reject)
**Why it matters:** This is the most dangerous drafting in the package. Read literally, it caps and time-bars all of the following:
- specific indemnities, such as the Ironquay indemnity and any we negotiate for DD-006 or tax;
- the tax covenant;
- completion-account or price-adjustment claims;
- leakage claims;
- breaches of pre-completion covenants;
- possibly even claims for fraud.

That empties every protection we negotiate below.

**Push back:** Reverse the default. Limitations should apply **only to Warranty Claims (other than Fundamental and Tax Warranties)** unless expressly extended. Add express carve-outs from all limitations, the exclusive-remedy clause and the non-reliance clause for:
- fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller, its officers or advisers;
- specific indemnities and the tax indemnity;
- price adjustment, Debt/Transaction Cost deductions and leakage;
- covenant breaches (pre-completion conduct, restraints, confidentiality).

Non-reliance should be confined to statements outside the SPA and Disclosure Letter. It should not purport to exclude claims for misleading or deceptive conduct based on the Seller's own disclosure materials. A non-reliance clause won't reliably exclude an ACL s 18 claim anyway, but we shouldn't concede the point.

### 3. General cap, de minimis and basket (negotiable, but tighten)
| Item | Seller | Comment | Suggested position |
|---|---|---|---|
| General cap | 20% (AUD 4.8m) | Within market range but low for a business with this many open issues | Open at 50%; landing zone 25–35%, or 20% if backed by W&I insurance and a retention |
| De minimis | AUD 25k | ~0.1% of price, so broadly market | AUD 10–15k, with **related claims aggregated** |
| Basket | AUD 250k, deductible | ~1.04% of price, so high end. Being deductible, we absorb the first AUD 250k of every loss | AUD 120–150k (0.5–0.6%), **tipping** (first dollar once exceeded) |
| Time limit | 18 months | Acceptable only if it covers two audit cycles | 24 months general; tax 7 years (to cover ATO amendment periods, which are longer for some taxpayers and unlimited for fraud or evasion) |

### 4. General disclosure (Schedule 7 / Disclosure Letter cl 1.1–1.2) (reject)
**Seller position:** The Seller discloses everything in the data room, the Accounts, the statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records".

**Why it matters:** This means any fact buried anywhere in the data room or a public register defeats a warranty claim, whether or not we could fairly have identified its significance. It turns the warranties into a due diligence exercise at our risk.

**Push back:**
- Delete general disclosure, or at most limit it to the Accounts.
- Disclosures should qualify warranties only if they are **fair, specific and in sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope** of the matter.
- Disclosure must be against identified warranties.
- No disclosure should qualify the Fundamental or Tax Warranties.
- The data room should be fixed by a USB/index annexed at signing, with no later updates disclosed against warranties without our consent.

### 5. Buyer knowledge bar (cl 8.3) (reject)
**Seller position:** No claim for any matter the Buyer *or its advisers* knew of, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."

**Why it matters:** This is an extreme anti-sandbagging clause based on constructive knowledge. It stacks on top of general disclosure, so the warranties become largely illusory.

**Push back:** Delete it. Better, include an express statement that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge. A fallback is to limit it to the **actual knowledge** of a short list of named Wattlebridge deal-team individuals, excluding adviser knowledge and constructive knowledge.

**Important consequence:** The Disclosure Letter makes reasonably specific disclosures on Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses, DD-006 and Sandbar. Those disclosures will likely defeat warranty claims on those matters even after we fix general disclosure. **Each known issue therefore needs to be dealt with by a condition, a price mechanism or a specific indemnity**, not left to the warranties. That is the approach in Part B.

---

## B. Specific identified exposures

### 6. Bluefen change-of-control consent (DD-002): about 30% of revenue (critical)
**Contradiction:** The SPA update says the consent is "addressed". Disclosure Letter item 2 says there is **no final written consent and no evidence the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied**.

**Problems with the Seller's mechanism:**
- "Reasonable endeavours" is a weak obligation.
- Deeming the condition satisfied on "delivery of the counterparty's written consent" means a consent with conditions attached, or one with the cl 11.3 conditions still outstanding, would count. We would then be obliged to complete while ~AUD 3.6m of revenue is at risk.

**Push back:**
- Make this a **condition precedent for the Buyer's sole benefit, waivable only by the Buyer**. It should be satisfied by unconditional written consent under cl 11.2, in a form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, with all cl 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived by Bluefen in writing. It must not impose adverse amended terms.
- Raise the Seller's obligation to **best or all reasonable endeavours**, with the Buyer having a right to participate in communications with Bluefen.
- Set a long-stop date with a Buyer termination right.
- Add a warranty, repeated at Completion, that no notice of termination or non-renewal has been received.
- Consider a MAC-type protection or price adjustment if Bluefen terminates or reduces volumes before Completion.

### 7. Riverlark Bank facility (DD-003): ~AUD 3.2m outstanding (critical)
**Seller position:** The release will be "provided following Completion".

**Why it matters:**
- The deal is debt-free/cash-free, so this facility is Debt and must be discharged from the price at Completion.
- A post-Completion release leaves security over the Company's assets in place, with nothing to compel the Seller to deliver it.
- Under the change-of-control clause (cl 8.1), Completion may itself be an event of default or a trigger for repayment, exposing the Company and its new owner.

**Push back:**
- Riverlark debt is to be **repaid from the Completion payment**, under a funds flow that pays Riverlark directly.
- Make delivery of a **payout letter** (stating the payout figure, per diem and undertaking to release) and an **executed deed of release** under cl 9.2 Completion deliverables.
- Require PPSR financing change statements to be lodged at or immediately after Completion, plus releases of any guarantees or real property security.
- The full payout amount, including break costs, accrued interest and fees, should be treated as Debt and deducted from the price.

### 8. Completion bonuses (DD-005): AUD 420k plus on-costs (high)
**Seller position:** The bonuses are "a matter for the Seller" and not itemised in the funds flow.

**Why it matters:** The bonuses are payable by the Company, through payroll, to its employees. Unless they are deducted from the price, the Buyer ends up funding them through the Company after Completion. On top of the bonus amounts:
- **NSW payroll tax** (currently 5.45%) likely applies;
- **superannuation guarantee** (12% from 1 July 2025) likely applies if the bonuses are ordinary time earnings;
- PAYG withholding and workers' compensation on-costs also apply.

Indicatively, on-costs could add roughly **AUD 70–80k**. This must be confirmed by tax and payroll advisers. Disclosure item 5 expressly does not address on-costs.

The continued-employment conditions also mean amounts could become payable after Completion, when we control the Company.

**Push back:**
- Define **Transaction Bonuses, including all employer on-costs**, as Transaction Costs or Debt, deducted from the price whether paid before or after Completion.
- Have the Company pay the bonuses through payroll at Completion using funds diverted from the Seller's proceeds, or deduct them and hold the amount for later payment.
- Add a specific indemnity for any bonus-related liability (including any further bonus arrangements not disclosed), outside the caps.
- If the deal is locked-box rather than completion accounts, these are **leakage**.

### 9. Ironquay IP (DD-004 / DD-010): SOW3 materials (high)
**Why it matters:** Under cl 7.3, title to the SOW3 Project Materials passes only on **cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open, there is no evidence of payment, and there is no confirmatory assignment. The Company may therefore **not own** IP it is using.

The Seller's indemnity covers only "the SOW3 payment". That is the smallest part of the risk. The real exposures are:
- infringement claims by Ironquay;
- loss of use;
- re-development costs;
- impacts on customer contracts that rely on the materials.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **condition or Completion deliverable** that the outstanding SOW3 fees are paid. The cost should be borne by the Seller, either paid before Completion and treated as leakage or deducted from the price.
- Require written confirmation from Ironquay that all SOW3 fees are paid, plus a **confirmatory deed of assignment** of all SOW3 Project Materials and IP, with moral rights consents from the individual authors.
- Expand the indemnity to cover **all Loss arising from the Company not owning or being unable to use the SOW3 materials, and any Ironquay claim**, outside the caps and time limits.
- Reject the statement that IP warranties are "settled under the general regime" (see item 13).

### 10. DD-006 export/privacy incident (high, with time sensitivity)
**Contradiction:** The SPA update calls this "not expected to be material". Disclosure Letter item 6 says it is unknown whether there was unauthorised access, what the scope is, or whether notification is required, and that the investigation is preliminary.

**Why it matters:** Around 1,240 records of personal information (names, emails, roles, activity timestamps) were sent to an unintended external address. If the Company is an APP entity (probable, given implied revenue of ~AUD 12m), the **Notifiable Data Breaches scheme** applies. A reasonable assessment of a suspected eligible data breach must be completed within **30 days** of awareness (Privacy Act s 26WH).

As at 22 September 2026 the investigation was still preliminary. Today is 5 November 2026, so **the 30-day window may already have expired**, depending on when the Company became aware. Late or missed notification is itself a compliance failure. Recent reforms have increased regulatory exposure, including civil penalty tiers and a statutory privacy tort.

**Push back:**
- **Immediate information request:** date of awareness, current investigation or forensic report, whether the link was accessed, any recall or deletion confirmation from the recipient, the notification decision and its reasoning, any OAIC or individual communications, and any insurer notification.
- Add a **specific indemnity for all Loss arising from DD-006**, outside the caps and basket and with a longer time limit. It should cover regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, notification and remediation costs, third-party and customer claims, and Bluefen or other contract consequences.
- Add pre-Completion covenants to complete the assessment and make any required notifications, in consultation with the Buyer.
- Consider a **retention or escrow** from the price.
- Confirm cyber insurance cover and whether the incident has been notified to insurers. Note that W&I insurance will exclude this known matter.

### 11. Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008 / DD-011): AUD 330k (medium–high)
**Why it matters:**
- The Seller calls these "ordinary course". Its own Disclosure Letter does not say so, describes them as "related", and says they should be read together.
- Three renewals at exactly AUD 110k each suggests **contract splitting**, possibly to stay below an approval threshold or a conduct-of-business consent threshold in the SPA.
- If Sandbar is a Seller-related party, these may be **value extraction**.

**Push back:**
- Request the contracts, approval records and the relationship between Sandbar and the Seller group.
- If related-party or entered after the locked-box date, the payments should be **leakage**, or the contracts should be terminated at the Seller's cost before Completion.
- Aggregate them for the purposes of the conduct-of-business restrictions.
- Add warranties that they are on arm's-length terms, terminable without penalty, and properly accrued in the Accounts.
- If the commitment isn't justified, adjust the price or require termination.

### 12. Title (DD-012) (high, but readily fixed)
The share register alone is not adequate evidence of title. Disclosure item 10 itself notes the Buyer has not verified title.

**Push back:**
- Verify against ASIC records, the constitution, and any shareholders' agreement (pre-emption rights, drag/tag).
- Run PPSR searches against the Seller and the Company.
- Confirm there are no options, convertible notes, ESOP awards or other rights to issue shares.
- Get Fundamental Warranties of clear, unencumbered title to fully paid shares, at 100% of the price (see item 1).
- Completion deliverables: share transfer forms, the share certificate (or a lost-certificate indemnity), a pre-emption waiver, and resignation/release deeds.

### 13. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime" (reject)
Tax and IP are high-risk areas here. Ironquay is a live IP gap, and the bonuses raise payroll tax and super issues.

**Push back:**
- A **standalone tax indemnity** for pre-Completion tax, outside the caps, with a 7-year limit and no disclosure against it.
- IP warranties that are not qualified by general disclosure, with key IP ownership warranties treated as quasi-fundamental (higher cap, longer period).

### 14. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) (lower; verify)
The Seller's position that neither the lease nor the Mossvale contract requires consent for a share sale may be correct. We should still check the definitions of "assignment" and "change in control" in each document, because some contracts deem a change of control to be an assignment.

**Push back:**
- Make giving the lease notification a pre-Completion covenant.
- Add a warranty that no material contract is triggered or terminable by the share sale except as specifically scheduled.

---

## C. Credit and recovery protection

Harbourglass Ventures appears to be an investment vehicle that may distribute the proceeds soon after Completion. Without credit support, the indemnities above may not be recoverable.

**Push back:** Require one or more of the following:
- a **retention or escrow** (e.g. 10–15% for 18–24 months, plus a specific DD-006 and Ironquay amount);
- a parent or fund guarantee;
- buy-side **W&I insurance**, which also helps justify a lower Seller cap but will exclude known matters, so the indemnities remain essential.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Priority | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title/capacity under general cap | **Critical** | Fundamental Warranties at 100% of price, 6+ years, no de minimis/basket, no disclosure |
| 2 | "Limitations apply to all Claims" / exclusive remedy / non-reliance | **Critical** | Limit to general Warranty Claims; carve out fraud, indemnities, tax, price mechanics, leakage, covenants |
| 3 | Bluefen consent (30% revenue) | **Critical** | Buyer-waivable CP: unconditional consent with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied; best endeavours; long-stop and walk right |
| 4 | Riverlark AUD 3.2m | **Critical** | Repay from Completion funds; payout letter and deed of release at Completion; PPSR discharges; treat as Debt |
| 5 | General disclosure and constructive-knowledge bar | **High** | Delete; fair and specific disclosure only; actual knowledge of named individuals at most |
| 6 | DD-006 privacy incident | **High / urgent** | Urgent NDB-timing information request; specific uncapped indemnity; pre-Completion covenants; retention |
| 7 | Bonuses AUD 420k plus on-costs | **High** | Transaction Costs/Debt including payroll tax, super and PAYG; deduct from price; indemnity |
| 8 | Ironquay SOW3 IP | **High** | Pay out AUD 180k at Seller cost; payment confirmation and confirmatory assignment as CP; full-loss indemnity |
| 9 | Tax/IP warranties | **High** | Standalone tax indemnity (7 years); strengthened IP warranties |
| 10 | Sandbar AUD 330k | **Medium–High** | Diligence the related-party nexus and contract splitting; leakage or termination at Seller cost |
| 11 | Cap / basket / time limits | **Medium** | Cap 25–35% (or 20% with W&I); tipping basket ~AUD 125–150k; de minimis AUD 10–15k with aggregation; 24 months |
| 12 | Title evidence | **Medium** | ASIC, PPSR, constitution and cap table verification; full title Completion deliverables |
| 13 | Lease / Mossvale | **Low** | Verify change-of-control definitions; notification covenant; no-trigger warranty |
| 14 | Recovery | **High** | Escrow/retention and/or guarantee; consider W&I |

**Immediate next steps:**
1. Send an information request on DD-006 today, given the NDB timing.
2. Request a Riverlark payout figure and a draft deed of release.
3. Obtain the Bluefen cl 11.2/11.3 correspondence.
4. Get Ironquay payment status confirmed directly.
5. Obtain the Sandbar contracts and related-party information.
6. Prepare a mark-up of cl 8.3, 9.3, 12 and 13 and Schedule 7 reflecting the above.

I can draft the issues list for the mark-up, the specific indemnity wording, or the information request if that would be helpful.
=== END ADVICE ===
